title: Typhoon Dujuan Threatens Asian Games as Nagoya Braces for Opening Weekend
excerpt: Tropical storm Dujuan is tracking toward Japan's Pacific coast with gusts up to 126 kph, forcing organisers to ready contingency plans — days after record rain forced athletes to evacuate their accommodation.
body:
• Tropical storm Dujuan was tracking toward central Japan on Thursday with sustained winds of 90 kph and gusts up to 126 kph, with forecasters warning it could strengthen into a typhoon and reach the Aichi-Nagoya coast on Monday, September 21.
  • Japan's chef de mission Kosei Inoue said some competitions have already been delayed or postponed by severe weather, and the Japanese Olympic Committee is holding emergency meetings to prepare response plans.
  • Thousands of athletes are housed aboard the cruise ship Costa Serena and in temporary container-style huts; Nagoya's mayor says protocols exist to evacuate athletes and move the ship offshore in typhoon-strength winds.
  • The 20th Asian Games open Saturday, September 19, with more than 17,000 competitors and officials — a larger gathering than the Olympics — while early events in soccer, basketball and volleyball are already underway.

The Storm Approaches

NAGOYA — Asian Games organisers are bracing for possible weather disruption in the opening days of the continent's biggest sporting event, with forecasters warning that tropical storm Dujuan could strengthen into a typhoon and reach Japan's main island as early as Sunday or Monday.

As of Thursday morning, Dujuan was located off Japan's Pacific coast and tracking northwest toward central Japan, where Nagoya sits, packing maximum sustained winds of 90 kph and gusts of up to 126 kph, according to Reuters. The 20th Asian Games officially begin with Saturday's opening ceremony, but soccer, basketball and volleyball competitions are already underway across the Aichi region.

Kosei Inoue, Japan's chef de mission for the Games and a senior executive board member of the Japanese Olympic Committee, addressed the threat at a press conference on Thursday. "Due to the heavy rain and severe weather, some competitions have already experienced delays or postponements, and there is also a possibility that a typhoon could approach on September 21," he told reporters. "Under these circumstances, we are holding thorough meetings within the JOC to ensure that we are fully prepared and capable of responding appropriately."

A Warning Shot Last Week

The typhoon threat arrives days after record rainfall exposed the fragility of the Games' unconventional accommodation plans. Torrential rains hit Nagoya and the surrounding region last week, forcing schools to close, train services to be suspended and several hundred athletes to briefly evacuate their accommodation, Reuters reported.

In a cost-saving departure from the traditional athletes' village, organisers scattered participants across temporary wooden container-style huts, hotel rooms and the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which usually carries holidaymakers but is now serving as a floating athletes' village for between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes and officials. More than 17,000 competitors and officials are expected in total — more than the Olympics — after organisers, who had initially planned for 15,000, scrambled to find beds for the rest.

The experiment has drawn sharp criticism. South Korean sports officials this week branded the facilities the "worst" accommodation ever at the Games and said the beds were too short, while a Korean Olympic committee official told AFP there was "a serious shortage of accommodation." India, for its part, went so far as to build its own replica container huts at home to acclimatise athletes before they flew to Japan.

What Happens If the Typhoon Hits

Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said protocols exist to temporarily evacuate athletes during severe weather and that the cruise ship could be moved offshore in the event of typhoon-strength winds, according to Reuters. The Asahi Shimbun quoted an unnamed sports federation official as saying of the ship, "All we can do is to pray that the worst-case scenario will not happen."

"Due to the heavy rain and severe weather, some competitions have already experienced delays or postponements, and there is also a possibility that a typhoon could approach on September 21."

— Kosei Inoue, Japan's chef de mission

For India's contingent, the stakes go beyond logistics. India arrives in Nagoya with genuine medal expectations across boxing, wrestling, athletics and cricket, and any disruption to the opening week's schedule could unsettle athletes who have spent years peaking for these Games. The Indian women's cricket team begins its title defence in a straight-knockout quarter-final against hosts Japan on Friday — a format that leaves no room for weather-related error.

A Test of a New Model

Organisers have defended the village-less model as a deliberate sustainability choice, arguing that major sporting events need more flexible infrastructure rather than expensive permanent villages with limited use after competition ends. OCA officials have called the accommodation "safe and functional." But the combination of record rain and a possible typhoon is now providing an unusually visible stress test of that philosophy — in the middle of typhoon season, which typically runs through September and October.

With the opening ceremony two days away and the Games running until October 4, organisers insist everyone will have a bed and that the party will go on. Whether Dujuan cooperates is now the question hanging over Nagoya.
nri_angle: India's athletes face schedule disruption and accommodation risk at the Nagoya Games, where the contingent arrived with real medal expectations across boxing, wrestling and cricket.
